reasoning: Long oo, and taa marbuta after ك is e. The word also means thorn, but fork is the normal Palestinian use.
Palestinian has a long oo (moot), not MSA mawt.
Taa marbuta after ب is e. The word is used in conversation for the 1948 catastrophe and also for a disaster in general.
ض is emphatic, so D. Long ii in the second syllable. Ordinary word for weak.

Form VIII imperative plural of ittaSal, with the doubled t and the i dropped before the plural ending u. ع + ال becomes 3ash-. Taa marbuta after ط is a. The exact imperative vowelling is less certain.
Short i in the first syllable and long aa. Taa marbuta after ن is e. Common Palestinian word for a cupboard or wardrobe.
Said in Palestinian as il-7amdilla, with no case ending. ع + السلامة assimilates to 3as-salaame. Taa marbuta after م is e. Also used to say welcome back or thank God you're safe.
Form I past, he-form, with short vowels throughout. Everyday word for sweeping.
Long oo. This is the collective noun, and a single banana is mooza.

The spelling هي is ambiguous between the presentative hayy (as in hayyo/hayyi, 'there he/she is'), and haay, 'this (f.)', spelled loosely. I chose the presentative to match 'here it is'. Not sure which the dictionary row intends.
In the abstract sense 'reality' this is an MSA-origin word, so ق tends to keep [q], as in il-waaqi3. Palestinians use it freely in conversation. A glottal waa'i3 is possible in casual speech.
Standard Palestinian na3saan with a long aa.
A relative by marriage, for example a sibling's or child's in-law. Long ii.
Unit noun of ghanam (sheep as a flock), meaning one sheep. Taa marbuta after م is e.
Simple CaCC noun.
ط is emphatic, so T, and the shadda doubles y. Means kind or good-hearted for a person. Tayyib is also the everyday 'okay'.
Palestinian usually has short i in the first syllable (sibaa7a), not MSA sabaaha. I treat the pharyngeal ح like ع, so taa marbuta is a.
ض is emphatic, so D. In speech fuDuuli usually means nosy or meddlesome, not just neutrally curious.

snaan is the plural of sinn, teeth, with -i for 'my'. A plural non-human noun takes feminine singular agreement, so btuuja3ni, from the initial-waw verb waja3 ('it hurts me'). The imperfect vowelling is the least certain part; btwajji3ni is also heard.
Form IV past, he-form, in common use. ط is emphatic, so T. The final alif maqsura is a. The imperative is 3Tiini.
il- assimilates to س. The w 'and' attaches to 3ashra. Taa marbuta after ر is a. The English is only a fragment, so I gave a clearer gloss.
Tal'a is one shot or bullet, with ق as a glottal stop in everyday speech. The phrase does not mean 'shooting' as an event, which is 'iTlaa' naar. Taa marbuta is a after ق and e after ي.
shu is the Palestinian 'what'. The vowel of il- drops after shu. ق in wa't is a glottal stop. Casual way to ask the time.
Palestinian been has a long ee, and the extended stem beenaat- takes the suffix -hum. The hyphen breaks the t+h so it is not read as th. Ramallah urban speech uses -hum rather than -hom.
ق is a glottal stop in wa't. The second wa't is joined to the preposition la-. Natural everyday phrase.
